title: I used Codex to make five poker bots that are supposed to feel like different people
author: kobefan1219
selftext:
I didn't want five copies of the same bot with slightly different difficulty settings.

each one starts with its own tendencies around aggression, risk and bluffing. they only use information a normal player could see, remember how I play across hands, and make small adjustments over time.

the adjustments are limited, so an aggressive bot shouldn't suddenly turn into a completely different player after ten hands.

it's not a solver or a GTO trainer. I mostly wanted the table to feel less like five random-number generators waiting for their turn.

they're all cats because apparently I make better design decisions when cats are involved.

built with codex. playable here:https://poker-ai-web.vercel.app/game

comments.author: GtoStrategy2026
comments.body: Love the approach of giving each bot a distinct personality. Since they adapt to how the player plays across hands, how many hands does it usually take for a bot to 'figure out' a super aggressive or super passive player?

replies.author: kobefan1219
replies.body:
Good question. There isn't really a hard switch where a bot suddenly has you figured out.

It starts building a read from the first hand, but I treat the first \~8 hands as pretty tentative. By around 12 hands it has enough of a read to lean into obvious tendencies, and the stats look a lot less noisy closer to 30.

So if someone is folding to pressure all the time or raising every other spot, the cats should start reacting sooner. But the adjustments are capped, so the aggressive cat won't suddenly turn into a perfect counter-bot after one bad run.

Still testing how that feels in practice, though.

replies.author: GtoStrategy2026
replies.body: That 12–30 hand window makes a lot of sense. Glad to hear the cats won't turn into GTO solvers after one aggressive orbit! Really cool project, man. Good luck with the testing
